newsitem.title: PERU: Peace broker asks Peru, rebels to put pride aside.
newsitem.headline: Peace broker asks Peru, rebels to put pride aside.

text.p: A leading mediator in Peru's 114-day-old hostage crisis called on the government and Marxist rebels to put pride aside in the search for the safe release of 72 captives held inside the Japanese ambassador's home in Lima.
"I call on both sides to think hard about the responsibility they have... about pride, about political objectives," Vatican representative Juan Luis Cipriani told reporters late on Wednesday.

Talks between Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) leader Nestor Cerpa Cartolini and government negotiator Domingo Palermo ended abruptly March 12 in disagreement over the MRTA's main demand for the release of about 450 jailed comrades.
But Cipriani, one of a three-man crisis mediation team, said the fact that face-to-face talks broke down nearly a month ago did not mean that moves to end the siege had ground to a halt.
"Don't think that because there are no formal meetings there are no talks," he said.

About 20 Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) fighters swept into a cocktail party at the diplomatic residence Dec. 17 and took more than 500 guests hostage. They gradually released all but 72 of their captives, keeping President Alberto Fujimori's brother, Pedro, two Cabinet ministers and the ambassadors of Japan and Bolivia.

Cipriani and fellow mediators Canadian Ambassador Anthony Vincent, and Red Cross official Michel Minnig, spent three hours inside the besieged home on Wednesday as part of their efforts to get the two sides back to the negotiating table.

President Fujimori, who refuses to contemplate releasing MRTA prisoners in exchange for the hostages, insisted on Wednesday that the storming of the diplomatic mansion did not signal a return to the regular rebel attacks of the early 1990s.

"In spite of the incident at the Japanese ambassador's residence, which has made news around the world, Peru's stability can be seen both in the economy and on the streets," he said at a conference of central bank officials from the Americas and Spain.
A key ally of Fujimori, Congress president Victor Joy Way, urged patience, saying the government would win less favourable terms if it rushed to an agreement.
"Our enemy is not time," Joy Way told reporters while on a visit to Shanghai, China. "The key element is patience. The first to lose patience will have less opportunity for a solution."
Fujimori has been under strong pressure from Tokyo to speed negotiations to free the hostages, who include about two dozen Japanese businessmen and diplomats.

The Japanese "are being very demanding," a government source close to Fujimori said. "Obviously there is great pressure from them but we have told them we are not going to cave in. We will not free the MRTA prisoners."

The source, speaking on condition of anonymity, said he believed Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto was under domestic political pressure to get the hostages freed soon, but "the (Peruvian) government's strategy is to wait."

Nonetheless, he said, indirect talks through the three-man mediation team had yielded progress. "There are advances. I think this could end in a relatively short time. It could end sooner than people think."
